newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: INTERVIEW - Portugal fund growth limited by tax.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Portugal fund growth limited by tax.

text.p: Assets under management by Portuguese investment funds should rise by around five percent in 1996, slow by European standards because growth continues to be hampered by the lack of tax incentives, a senior official said.

Jose Carlos Maia, chairman of the Portuguese Association of Investment Fund Management (APFIN) told Reuters that funds under management should reach some 2,850 billion escudos ($18.3 billion) by the year's end if, as expected, the five percent growth seen in the first half of the year were maintained.
But the five percent was little when compared with the 20 percent jump seen in Spanish investment funds over the same period, he said in an interview.

The increase in Spain would take funds under management there to 23 percent of the country's gross domestic product (GDP) against 18 percent at the start of the year when the equivalent level in Portugal had been 17 percent.
Maia said that the APFIN had presented a proposal to the government to improve the tax treatment of the funds.
The plan -- Individual Savings Plan (PIP) -- was aimed at making it fiscally more attractive to invest in investment funds rather than directly in stocks and bonds, he said.
Attention also needed to be paid to making it more attractive to invest locally rather than abroad, he added.

The PIP would have a life of eight to 12 years. It would be exempt from corporation tax and 50 percent of its funds would be invested in state debt to reduce risk and help the government place its paper, Maia said.
He said more needed to be done to "educate" the investor in the advantages of investing with a fund.

"There are advantages in professional management...because the investor need have less fear of the risk (while) that way investments are more influenced by the real economic situation of the country," he said.
Maia said that he saw a growing trend towards investment in risk funds with their use of the derivatives market.
The percentage of assets invested in shares and fixed-rate bonds rose from 9.3 percent at the end of 1995 to 10.2 percent in the first half of 1996, he said.
